articles.title: I'm not a fan of Deno's security model (2024)
articles.content: I’m not a fan of Deno’s security model (published on August 31, 2024) this has been bothering me for a while now, so I want to write down my thoughts so I can get it out of my head and move on. we’re gonna talk about how Deno approaches security, specifically with its permissions system, and why I think this approach is fundamentally insecure and misleading. wait, what’s Deno? Deno is a language runtime for JavaScript. it consists of a standard library, a package manager, a TypeScript transpiler and a bunch of other stuff that’s not important for our story. it’s not a JavaScript implementation , so it does not interpret or compile JavaScript, it reuses V8 for that. one of the flagship features of Deno is its permission system (it’s under the “Secure by default” header on their landing page ). the idea is simple: as JS code running in Deno needs the standard library to access the outside world, Deno can choose which accesses it allows or disallows, so when you run shell deno run --allow-read = /tmp/dir --allow-run = uname code.ts the standard library will only allow code.ts to read /tmp/dir and run uname . additionally, a program can request permissions at runtime, so code like typescript const r = { name : "read" , path : "/tmp/dir" } as const ; await Deno . permissions . request ( r ); will display a nice little prompt in the terminal: ┌ ⚠️ Deno requests read access to "/tmp/dir". ├ Requested by `Deno.permissions.request()` API. ├ Run again with --allow-read to bypass this prompt. └ Allow? [y/n/A] (y = yes, allow; n = no, deny; A = allow all read permissions) > and you can grant or refuse it. (aside: I really miss this feature in browser extensions. currently, if your extension needs potential access to any website, it needs to request actual access to all the websites, which is less than ideal) if you like puzzles, this is the point where you can stop and think about what could go wrong with this system. the prompts problem of the two specific issues I want to point out this is the less severe one. we’ll discuss it first because this was the first thing I noticed and it kinda immediately irked me when I first read about this. (if you’re only interested in the more juicy part, you can skip to the next section ). so, this nice little prompt is displayed in the terminal. it’s not, like, a PolKit GUI window or anything, it’s just text on stdout waiting for input from stdin. this is a wild thing to do. you see, terminal has a somewhat weird API. most of the commands / requests application can send to the terminal are sent in-band, by printing them to stdout. terminal can then reply by sending data to stdin. as Deno allows programs to print arbitrary data to stdout and read from stdin without requiring any permissions or doing any filtering, malicious code can send arbitrary commands to the terminal. it’s usually okay, because terminals won’t, like, execute shell commands just because stdout told them to, you’re supposed to be able to freely cat file

articles.title: Declarative Dragging
articles.content: Declarative Dragging Joshua Horowitz , Andrew Blinn , Jeffrey Heer ★ Best Paper Award , UIST 2026 PDF paper video demos explorable supplement What if making a diagram draggable was as simple as specifying what it can become? Drag-and-drop makes the digital graspable. But designing bespoke drag interactions involves a lot of fiddly code to handle geometry, feedback, and animations. As a result, many people, from educators to game designers, mathematicians to creative tool builders, often don't bother. Declarative dragging inverts the problem. Rather than programming all that visual behavior directly, you simply say, for each element you want to make draggable, which future states of your application dragging it should lead to. Our system speculatively renders those states to work out where things can go, then combines these possible worlds into a smooth, responsive drag-and-drop interaction. Our goal with this project is to let people keep working within the semantic worlds they inhabit, while helping them turn the rules of their worlds into rich tactile interactions in ours. A five-minute video introducing declarative dragging. How it works D2 is model-driven : An interface author makes an element draggable by specifying which future model states should be accessible by dragging it. An engine speculatively renders these states to view trees, extracts the position of the dragged element in each of these renderings, and uses these to synthesize a drag-and-drop interaction, all without detailed work required by the interface author. Dragology is a library implementing “declarative dragging”: a new way for interface developers to make higher-quality drag-and-drop interactions with less work. Dragology enables model-driven dragging. To provide greater expressive range and customizability, D2 is composable : simple model-driven drag-and-drop behaviors can be combined to create more complex ones, and modifiers can layer features like floating, snapping, and transitions. For more details, see the paper . Dragology demos We implemented D2 in a library called Dragology , built for SVG interfaces on the web. algebra twisted trees bézier curve braid card piles face trominoes sprouting tree See our demo gallery for many more interactives built with Dragology. Where it came from Back in 2022, I had a prototype of a game aimed at making math more tangible, a long-running obsession of mine. It had a lot going for it, but the fundamental mechanic, based on selecting transformations from a menu, lacked the juicy tactility I craved. articles.title: Outlook.com Is Quietly Rejecting Email from Domains Without DMARC
articles.content: Since November 5, 2026, Microsoft's consumer mail service has been turning away some of the email from domains that don't publish a DMARC record. If your company emails customers, vendors or applicants with outlook.com, hotmail.com, live.com or msn.com addresses, some of that mail may be bouncing right now. Nobody announced it. The fix is one DNS record. Key takeaways Outlook.com, Hotmail, Live and MSN now refuse part of the mail from domains that have no DMARC record. It hits ordinary, low-volume senders, not only the bulk senders Microsoft's published rules cover. Only some messages bounce, so "my mail is getting through" doesn't mean your domain is safe. The fix is a single TXT record, v=DMARC1; p=none , which changes nothing about how other receivers treat your mail. What the bounce looks like The sender gets a bounce like this one, followed by a bracketed server name and ID that differ per message: 550 5.7.1 Message rejected: Message lacks SPF/DKIM/DMARC Auth Records (AS9031519) On the first day, the same rejection came back without the (AS9031519) code: 550 5.7.1 Message rejected: Message lacks SPF/DKIM/DMARC Auth Records The wording suggests something is badly broken. Usually it isn't. The domains we have seen bounced mostly had working SPF, and many had DKIM too. What they were missing was the DMARC record that ties the two to the From address. What changed Microsoft does have published sender rules. Since May 2025, domains that send more than 5,000 messages a day to Outlook.com have had to pass SPF, DKIM and DMARC, or get 550 5.7.515 Access denied . That rule is aimed at marketers and bulk senders, and most small businesses rightly assumed it didn't apply to them. This new rejection is different in the ways that matter: It reaches small senders. A one-line reply from a small office can bounce. It wasn't announced. As of November 6, Microsoft has published nothing about it: no postmaster notice, no blog post, no service-health entry. It doesn't say what failed. A 5.7.515 bounce lists the SPF, DKIM and DMARC results. This one only says records are missing. We first saw these bounces in our own outbound logs on November 5. Public reports from other administrators started appearing the same day. Why it's easy to miss Microsoft refuses only part of the mail from an affected domain. One message to a Hotmail address goes through, the next one bounces, and a resend may succeed. That inconsistency is what makes this one dangerous: the person who sent the message sees a bounce full of acronyms, assumes a glitch, and moves on. The customer on the other end never knows a message was sent. If your business depends on reaching people at personal addresses (patients, homeowners, applicants, parents, members), the cost is quiet. Invoices that don't arrive, appointment confirmations that never land, replies that look like you ignored someone. Is your domain affected? Your domain is exposed if it has no DMARC record. articles.title: Goldman Sachs is pulling Claude Code from its bankers and traders
articles.content: In July, Goldman's tech chief was praising the tools traders built with AI coding agents. New internal guidance hands those agents back to the engineers, weeks before Goldman takes Anthropic public. Goldman Sachs has restricted Anthropic's Claude Code and Microsoft's GitHub to its engineers, cutting off traders and bankers who used the tools to track client flows and build market models. The bank barred its Hong Kong bankers from Claude in April and is now a lead underwriter on Anthropic's IPO. Most traders and bankers at Goldman Sachs can no longer use AI coding tools at work. Internal guidance updated in October restricts Anthropic's Claude Code and Microsoft's GitHub to the bank's engineers, Bloomberg News reported , following a review of productivity and risk concerns. Strats, who work across trading, quantitative research and software engineering, still have access, according to a second person familiar with the matter. The change has frustrated some traders, a person familiar with the matter told Bloomberg. They had been using the tools to monitor client trading flows, model market moves and positions, and put together written and graphic material. Goldman spokesperson Nick Carcaterra said the bank makes certain AI tools available to staff "to determine the best use cases" across the firm. Argenti was praising trader-built tools in July As recently as July, chief information officer Marco Argenti was talking up "vibe coding" by Goldman's non-technical employees. He told Bloomberg that traders and bankers had built tools with AI and passed them to the firm's engineers, of whom there are about 12,000, to be improved. That arrangement let the people closest to a problem build a first version without waiting for engineering time. It also meant thousands of employees without engineering training were running software that writes and executes code, on the same machines they use to handle client information. At a conference in Turin last month, Argenti described Goldman's AI adoption in waves and said developers, more than 12,000 of the bank's roughly 47,000 staff, had made up the first. The October guidance limits the coding agents to that group. Goldman restricted Claude in Hong Kong in April In April, Goldman removed Claude from its internal AI platform for bankers in Hong Kong. The Financial Times reported that the bank had read its contract with Anthropic strictly , and an Anthropic spokesperson said Claude had never been officially supported in Hong Kong. ChatGPT and Gemini remained available there. JPMorgan removed Claude from its Hong Kong approved list in June. The Hong Kong restriction was based on location and contract terms, and the new one is based on role. Goldman's in-house AI assistant, which uses models from several companies, is still available across the firm. The restriction applies to third-party agents that can write and run code by themselves. By default, all 6 routed experts per layer ( Top-6 ) are evaluated without pruning. CPU Cache & SIMD Kernel Patches ( +77% prefill, +53% decode): Replaces single-column quantized matrix-vector loops during prompt prefill with a 4-level register ( ZMM AVX-512BW) + L1D ( 32 KB ) + L2 ( 1 MB ) + L3 ( 64 MB ) multi-column ( {8,4,3,2} ) tiling schedule ( 25.0 -> 44.36 tok/s on 16-core Zen 5), register-stationary MQA8 FlashAttention, and non-temporal _MM_HINT_NTA MoE streaming so cold expert weights do not evict hot KV cache lines from L3. articles.title: systemd loves Rust
articles.content: Nov 3, 2026 6 min read systemd ❤️ Rust By Christian Brauner and Lennart Poettering systemd recently merged support for Rust . Going forward it will be possible to write systemd components in Rust in addition to C. The choice to integrate another core language into a large and established project is always contentious. We have seen the same when Rust was adopted as an additional language for the Linux kernel . As we know by now, that has mostly been successful. Rust support in systemd has two possible meanings: leaf components (individual binaries) root components (Rust in the fundamental libsystemd-shared.so shared library itself) The project came to the conclusion that (1) is acceptable while (2) is (currently) not, as the scope and requirements are very different between these two options. Rust in systemd Shared Libraries 🥺 Option (2) is complicated. The details are best left to another blog post but the gist is that we require first-class shared library support in Rust. In the Rust community, this is often referred to as the “stable ABI problem,” which is a well-known and long-standing issue . Until that is available we cannot integrate Rust into root components, otherwise every shared library and many binaries would be bloated by duplicated Rust code. Static linking for a project like systemd that is split into many tiny components (> 180 binaries currently) is simply not practical or desirable. Generally, static linking works for the leaves of the OS but the core often has different requirements. Rust in systemd Binaries 😍 Option (1) means that the shared code remains C-only, and we wrap this functionality as Rust crates. The crates are then used for Rust binaries. This allows us to consume all the core API functions uniformly across all components independent of whether they are written in Rust or in C. Key Design Decisions When Rust was accepted into systemd, the project adopted the following principles : Uniform Access to Core APIs. The systemd shared library has a wide range of helpers that provide features and security that are far beyond what either libc or any Rust crate provide. The clearest example is systemd’s chase*() family of functions. It is a purely fd-based API for path lookup that the whole tree uses. Any new kernel feature that improves on the security and reliability of path lookup is immediately adopted and securely abstracted. There is no equivalent to any of this in core Rust. Uniform Behavior. Binaries in C and in Rust look and behave identically in how they parse options, display help, and output error messages. It is inherently unacceptable for binaries in Rust to spuriously differ from systemd’s C binaries. The user should never have to care about the specific language a binary is implemented in. It simply shouldn’t affect behavior. Uniform Build System. Like most contemporary programming languages, Rust comes with its own build and dependency management ecosystem: cargo . articles.title: A bit about email
articles.content: A bit about email 2026-11-06 Before you torch and pitchfork me, I'm aware most of this is simplified and doesn't go into edge cases, even though the internet is composed entirely of edge cases. Otherwise, I'd be writing a whole book. First, some terminology; A typical email will past through many different components on it's way to the recipient: 1. Sender's MUA [Via SMTP on port 465] 2. Sending MSA 3. Sending MTA [Via SMTP on port 25] 4. Receiving MTA 5. Receiving LDA and message store [Via IMAP] 7. Receiver's MUA (These aren't all necessarily different machines or even different programs, but it is helpful to give a name for each step.) The mail user agent (MUA) runs on the user's computer and is what they use to send or read messages. Let's say they send something: that message will be uploaded to to the submission agent (MSA) which checks the user's password before handing off to the mail transfer agent (MTA). The transfer agent's job is to talk to the other mail servers and get the message to the receiving side's MTA. Once received, it's given to the local delivery agent (LDA) to be stored until the recipient checks their email. The name "LDA" is non-standard, but I use it to avoid having four different abbreviations differing by a single letter. The reason for this structure is that when the system was being designed (around 1980), most organizations could only afford a single server. Maintenance was a full time job and updates often required multiple days of downtime. A well-connected computer might have dedicated single-digits megabit/second link that worked half the time. This forced the MTA and MUA distinction: if the recipient's server isn't up when the email is set, the sending MTA will save the message and re-attempt delivery later. This way, short outages don't cause bounced mail. Since the mail client is an interactive program the user runs, a separate message store is needed to keep the email until it can be read. Most MTAs are configured to continue retrying a message for five days, usually with exponential backoff: mine will wait 5 minutes after the first failure, and increase the interval to one hour during prolonged outages. The MSA and LDA have always existed in some capacity, but have gotten a lot more complicated when people started accessing email from their own computers instead or remotely logging onto the server. SMTP Most communication happens over the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol, including MTA-MTA delivery. To narrow it down a bit, I'll pretend do be an MTA sending email to blog@maurycyz.com. The first step is to look up the receiving MTA for that domain: # dig MX maurycyz.com [snip] maurycyz.com. 300 IN MX 1 smallcrow.com. articles.title: How are you dealing with all the negative side effects of AI on the web?
articles.content:
It seems to me that the AI hype killed the web for good, but not for the reasons we immediately associate with it.

Search engines now rank links full of slop at the top, which ironically make LLM summaries acceptable, not because they are better than what we had before (they are not), but because they at least mention the good links which are now buried at the bottom of the page. Also, they've been rate limiting ordinary users like crazy: more often than I'd like to, Google and DuckDuckGo now either show me either an error message or tell me to wait a bit. Sometimes I waste at least a minute refreshing the page and waiting for a result.

I also can't browse GitHub freely without being logged in. Anubis is now everywhere, occasionally blocking me. I feel like my productivity has actually gone down thanks to all of that.

Edit: I see that most of the replies here are suggesting relying less on the web and going after more fundamental resources, which are great suggestions, don’t get me wrong! But a book from 5 years ago will not help you understand why your custom firmware doesn’t boot in your 1-year old mobile chipset. A existing bug report on the web probably will. Not quite my predicament at the moment, but something very similar for which the web seemed to work just fine before the AI craze.

NetBSD is the only open-source operating system in development that I know of, that doesn't include AI slop. At least for now? I decided to give it a go and try to install it on the Pi. How hard can it be? It turns out, not that much. I made a small guide on how I did it, maybe it helps someone. I assume you're preparing the SD card for the Pi on Linux. Get the latest image for arm64: https://nycdn.netbsd.org/pub/NetBSD-daily/netbsd-11/latest/evbarm-aarch64/binary/gzimg/arm64.img.gz Get the latest Raspberry Pi UEFI firmware: https://github.com/pftf/RPi4/releases Get Balena's Etcher (if you don't have it): https://etcher.balena.io/#download-etcher Extract Insert the microSD card in your laptop (I used cheap USB SD card reader). Extract the Etcher, enter it's directory and launch it (as a regular user): $ cd balenaEtcher-linux-x64/ $ ./balena-etcher In the UI, select the "Flash from file" option and find the previously extracted NetBSD arm64 image. For destination select the SD card (make sure it's really the SD card! In my case it was on /dev/sda). Flash the image (give sudo access). Extract it: $ mkdir rpi_firmware $ unzip -d rpi_firmware RPi4_UEFI_Firmware_v1.53.zip Create a directory for the NetBSD boot partition mount: $ sudo mkdir -p /mnt/netbsd-boot Mount the SD card's first partition there: $ sudo mount -t vfat /dev/sda1 /mnt/netbsd-boot Copy all the files from the rpi_firmware directory to /mnt/netbsd-boot (overwrite everything). $ sudo cp -r rpi_firmware /mnt/netbsd-boot/ This step is needed so the UEFI BIOS can actually boot the NetBSD partitions on the SD card. Unmount the partition: $ sudo umount /mnt/netbsd-boot Now you can insert the SD card into your Raspberry Pi. Turn it on and press ESC to enter the UEFI setup menu. Open Boot Maintenance Manager -> Boot Options -> Change Boot Order, move the SD card to the top (with the + key), then choose Commit Changes and Exit. NetBSD should now boot. It will start with resizing the root filesystem. When finished, you can login with "root". Set a password with 'passwd'. It's recommended to create a user right away, but you can do that later too: $ useradd -m -G wheel YOUR_USER $ passwd YOUR_USER Make WiFi work Now let's connect to the WiFi. If we type 'ifconfig', we can't see the wireless adapter there. That's a problem. In dmesg however we can see that the kernel recognized it and found its driver, but couldn't autoconfigure it: $ dmesg | grep -iE 'bwfm|firmware|sdio|wifi' bwfm0: Found firmware file: brcmfmac43455-sdio.bin bwfm0: autoconfiguration error: NVRAM file not available Let's fix this: $ cd /libdata/firmware/if_bwfm $ ln -s brcmfmac43455-sdio.raspberrypi,4-model-b.txt "brcmfmac43455-sdio.Raspberry Pi 4 Model B.txt" Reboot. ifconfig now shows the bwfm0 device. Let's configure our WiFi access point. Edit the rc.conf: Add this to the bottom: ifconfig_bwfm0="up" wp

articles.title: Nspawn 3.0: A Docker-compatible Engine API for systemd-nspawn containers
articles.content: Since 2.0.0 2.0.0 gave the machines that mount docker’s socket a read-only Docker API, enough for Traefik or Dozzle to find them. 3.0.0 serves the API with its changes, on the host too. In between: 2.1.0: published ports answer over IPv6 too, and -p takes IPv6 addresses. 2.2.0: fixes for what came up moving a whole server of compose projects to nspawn. compose got anonymous volumes, networks made again when their definition changes, down SERVICE and a start that brings up what a service depends on. 2.3.0: every layer is applied inside the tree it is extracted into and checked against the digest its image names for it. 2.3.1: packages on apt.nspawn.org (Debian 13+, Ubuntu 24.04+) and rpm.nspawn.org (Fedora 44+). 2.4.0: -p PORT takes a free port of the host, and a pull of an image index picks the entry for the host’s platform. The Docker Engine API on the host The host’s socket is /run/nspawn/api.sock , opened by nspawn-api.socket . Its main purpose is compatibility: tools that manage containers through the Docker API, like GitLab Runner’s docker executor, can use nspawn’s machines instead. nspawn is still the command line for managing them, but the docker command works against the socket too. The packages ship the socket turned off. Once it listens, nspawn-api.service starts on the first connection: 1 $ sudo systemctl enable --now nspawn-api.socket With DOCKER_HOST pointing at it, the docker command talks to nspawn: 1 2 3 4 5 6 $ export DOCKER_HOST = unix:///run/nspawn/api.sock $ docker run --rm -it alpine sh $ docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx $ docker exec -it web sh $ docker cp web:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf . $ docker rm -f web The API server is a client of the bus service, as the command line is. Everything it does is a method of org.nspawn , under the same polkit actions: reads and waits need org.nspawn.inspect , logs and changes need org.nspawn.manage . Every user can connect, but polkit is never asked to prompt, since nothing on a socket can answer an authentication agent. Root can do everything, and any other user needs a polkit rule, like nspawn-wheel.rules , which the packages ship as an example. As with the docker group, a user with org.nspawn.manage is root on the host: a machine runs commands as root and can mount any host path. What one socket’s clients hold at once (connections, log and event streams, waits, attaches, execs) is bounded, and a user other than root gets a share of each, so no user can keep the others or root out. Clients that only look at /run/docker.sock find it with a drop-in, on a host where nothing else has that path: 1 2 3 $ sudo mkdir -p /etc/systemd/system/nspawn-api.socket.d $ printf '[Socket]\nSymlinks=/run/docker.sock\n' | sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/nspawn-api.socket.d/symlink.conf $ sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl restart nspawn-api.socket What the API serves It answers in the shapes of API 1.51, and of the versions down to 1.24 that clients ask for. articles.title: Unattended reboots with encrypted disks
articles.content: Do you run a small home server or NAS holding your precious photos and sensitive documents? If so, I suppose the drives are encrypted, right? But then… can you reboot the machine without manually entering a passphrase before being able to access your files again? If you answered yes to the questions above—which is common for convenience—that implies the encryption keys live in the machine which… kinda defeats the purpose of disk encryption, doesn’t it? A thief can break into your house, lift the whole box (they are small these days, huh), plug it in elsewhere, and gain free rein over your files. So, which one is it? Simplicity and reliability by allowing automatic reboots or data protection by keeping the key in your head? With ZKeys—a little new project I’m launching today—you can have your cake and eat it too. A blog on operating systems, programming languages, testing, build systems, my own software projects and even personal productivity. Specifics include FreeBSD, Linux, Rust, Bazel and EndBASIC. TL;DR ZKeys is a managed service that stores encryption passphrases off-site. Client machines fetch the encryption keys from the service and keep those keys alive (unlocked) via periodic keepalive messages. If the server stops receiving those messages for a long period of time (e.g. because it has been unplugged as part of theft), access to the key is automatically locked. You get automatic, passwordless reboots while keeping your data protected against real incidents. Storytime About a year ago, I was reinstalling my FreeBSD home server to act as my NAS after a short stint with a Synology box . During that process, I decided to enable encryption for the ZFS data pool. But as I did that, I faced the question: how do I allow the machine to automatically serve my data after a reboot? I could put the key in a local file, which FreeBSD supports via the keylocation ZFS option, but that would render disk encryption pretty much useless. So I had an idea: what if I put the key on a different machine away from my house? I could then make the NAS fetch the key to mount the drives. And if someone stole the server, I could wipe the remote key and make the data unreadable before they could plug it back in. I did post this to Twitter and there was some interest in the idea: But… did you notice the problem with what I said above? Wiping the key by hand after noticing something is wrong is problematic because the gap between those two events may be large. What if I’m on a long vacation and I have no means of noticing that the machine has been stolen? Game over. So I refined the idea: what if I had a service that stored the key remotely and required the consuming machine to send it frequent pings to keep the key unlocked? This way, if the machine were stolen, it’d likely be offline for more than a few minutes and the service could automatically determine that something is wrong and lock the key from future accesses. And that’s precisely what ZKeys does. Zero-knowled

Introducing Project Steadfast 07·11·2026 Recently I wrote about an idea that’s been floating around in my mind for a long time - the ability to do metaprogramming in Ruby by manipulating Ruby ASTs, similar to the macro capabilities of languages such as Lisp or Elixir. The use of eval (in its different variations) is a common metaprogramming technique in Ruby that consists of generating code at runtime from dynamically constructed strings. This is often done for performance reasons: ERB compiles templates into optimized code by generating pieces of Ruby source code then putting them together and calling eval ; In Rails, the same technique is used for implementing features such as associations, or scaffolding. With eval , we can avoid paying the performance overhead that’s often associated with using DSLs in Ruby. But using eval in a highly-dynamic context may also be error-prone, limited, and potentially vulnerable to injection attacks. Having to painstakingly construct strings containing Ruby source code can be an arduous task, especially if you want to compile a DSL into efficient code, as in the case of ERB, or my own Papercraft . In Papercraft, HTML is generated using a DSL. Here’s an example: header { p { strong ( repo_name ) } p ( repo_description ) p { code ( clone_command ) } } While this kind of code may be used to generate HTML using the builder pattern , which is the traditional way of implementing DSLs in Ruby, it introduces a significant performance overhead. That is why in Papercraft I chose to implement a compiler that takes the code above and compiles it into the optimized form: __buffer__ . < < ( "

" ). < < ( ERB :: Escape . html_escape (( repo_name ))) . < < ( "

articles.title: Virtualized Redox: from Virtio-FS to Cloud Hypervisor, and beyond
articles.content: By MJ Pooladkhay on Sunday, November 8, 2026 Hello, Reader! I’m MJ Pooladkhay , and for the past couple of months I have been building a Virtio-FS driver for Redox OS and, more recently, getting Redox to run on Cloud Hypervisor . The driver is merged into the base repository , where most Redox drivers and system components live. The kernel, bootloader and driver changes that let Redox boot to a shell on Cloud Hypervisor are merged too ( details below ). Both are fun pieces of work on their own, but they are really the first steps of a bigger effort with two directions: Redox as a guest : Redox runs as a cloud server, starting with Cloud Hypervisor, without the legacy PC hardware it used to depend on in QEMU. Most of this post is about this one. Redox as a host : Redox runs virtual machines itself. This one is still a proposal, and I’ll go over it at the end of this post . The guest work is generously funded by NGI Zero Commons and NLnet as part of the Virtualized Redox grant. Why run Redox as a guest? Most Internet-facing software today runs in virtual machines, either in the cloud or on edge servers close to its users. Web servers, databases, API backends and microservices spend all day handling input from strangers, and that is where a memory-safe microkernel-based operating system has the most to offer: A smaller, safer base. Redox is written in Rust, and its drivers, filesystems and network stack run as separate userspace processes instead of inside the kernel ( microkernel architecture ). A bug may hang or crash only that process, not the whole system, and the code running with highest system privileges stays small. Sandboxing built in. With capability-based security , each service can be limited to the files, sockets and devices it actually needs ( more on that below ). Hardware becomes the host’s problem. On bare metal, Redox needs a driver for every disk controller, network card and chipset it meets. Inside a VM, the host deals with the hardware, and Redox only needs a handful of VirtIO drivers. That makes a VM one of the quickest paths to running Redox in the real world, and real-world use is the best way to prove it as a secure platform. This is the direction the project set in its development priorities : Redox as a secure host for web services, first as a private or edge server, and eventually as a multi-tenant cloud server where each tenant is isolated from others. How Virtualization Works The easiest way I know to think about a hypervisor is as an operating system whose processes are operating systems. A process runs directly on the CPU until it needs the kernel, for a system call, a page fault or a timer tick, and then the kernel takes over for a moment. A guest OS runs directly on the CPU in the same way, until it does something that only the hypervisor is allowed to handle. articles.content: Browser automation for AI agents: open pages, read them as an accessibility tree, and act on elements from the shell. agent-browser is a native Rust CLI that gives an AI agent a browser it can drive one command at a time. snapshot returns the page as compact text with a ref such as @e1 for each element. The agent acts on a ref, reads the page again to check the result, and repeats. The browser stays open between commands, so each step is one short shell call. npm install -g agent-browser agent-browser install # download Chrome for Testing (first time only) Homebrew: brew install agent-browser , then agent-browser install . Linux: agent-browser install --with-deps also installs the browser's system libraries. No install: npx agent-browser open example.com . Project installs, building from source, upgrade , and doctor are covered in Installation . agent-browser open example.com agent-browser snapshot -i # interactive elements, each with a ref agent-browser click @e1 # act on a ref from that snapshot agent-browser get url # check the result agent-browser close The snapshot for example.com : - link "Learn more" [ref=e1] Refs describe the page at the time of the snapshot. After navigation or a DOM change, take a new snapshot before using refs again. CSS selectors, text, XPath, and semantic locators also work, for example agent-browser find role button click --name "Submit" . See Selectors . A click fails, instead of reporting success, when the target is hidden, disabled, outside the viewport, or covered by another element such as a consent banner. Dismiss the covering element, take a new snapshot, and retry. The full walkthrough is in the quick start . The CLI sends each command to a background daemon that starts on the first command and controls the browser over the Chrome DevTools Protocol. Each --session gets its own daemon and browser. By default, the daemon closes a headless browser and exits after one hour without commands, saving state first when session persistence is configured. Chrome for Testing is the default browser. articles.title: Wandrd’s Magnetic Camera Straps Are My New Favorite Accessory
articles.content: More than a decade ago, Peak Design rethought the humble camera strap. This was a necessary development. When you buy a camera, manufacturers almost always toss in a chintzy, uninspired strap with their logo on it. These cheap straps have cheap mounting systems that make it hard to quickly remove the strap from the camera when you need to, like when you're attaching your camera to a tripod or gimbal and you’d rather not have a dangling strap whacking you in the face. Peak Design solved this with its Anchor Links system , small circular nubs you leave attached to camera eyelets that make detaching or even swapping straps easy. The quick-connect mechanism is now the de facto industry standard and has inspired countless copycats. Now, Wandrd has outdone that design using magnets . “We're photographers ourselves, so we're constantly ideating, tinkering, thinking of ways that things can be better,” Ryan Cope, Wandrd cofounder, tells WIRED. “A camera strap like this has been at the back of our minds for a while.” Wandrd —known for its camera bags —launched its Magnetic Camera Strap system on Thursday. It features a circular anchor similar to Peak Design, called “Torus Links.” The anchors attach to your camera’s eyelets and are rated to carry up to 198 pounds—so unless you're bench-pressing your camera, they'll do the job. If the cord does start to wear down over time, you'll first see yellow under the black fabric—a sign you should replace the Torus Link. If it's red, you should stop using the link immediately—a warning system borrowed from Peak Design. (Wandrd offers a two-year warranty.) Unlike Peak Design's anchors, the Wandrd anchors look like donuts, with a hole in the middle. When you attach the strap, the embedded magnets guide the Torus Link into the strap's CoreLock mechanism, which pinches into the hole to secure the camera body. The magnets make connecting a strap easier, and they keep the strap fastened to the anchor, but you can’t just pull the strap off like you’re pulling a MagSafe accessory on your phone. You’ll need to use the strap’s dual-pinch mechanism to remove it from the Torus Link, a design that’s more secure. The Torus Link is the donut-shaped object that attaches to your camera. On the right is the Magnetic CoreLock at the end of the strap. Pinch the top and bottom of this mechanism and let the magnets guide the strap into the Torus Link. Usually, I use Peak Design's Leash and, instead of taking off the strap, I bunch it up in my hand when it's not around my neck. It's not that it's hard to remove—it's just an extra step I have to think about. articles.summary: 苹果发布搭载 M6 芯片的 14 英寸 MacBook Pro，但 M5 款正在促销，Wired 认为升级未必划算。

articles.title: World Models Will Soon Be Inescapable. Here’s What You Need to Know
articles.content: Moving AI from text to 3D space, world models simulate real-world physics to teach robots and autonomous cars how to navigate reality.
articles.summary: 世界模型将 AI 从文本扩展到 3D 空间，模拟真实物理，用于训练机器人和自动驾驶汽车。

articles.title: The Fridge-Hacking Spree Is an Internet-of-Things Wake-Up Call
articles.content: Escalating hacks affecting blood labs and grocery stores show the very real risks to critical infrastructure that come from basic security lapses involving internet-connected devices.
articles.summary: 针对血库和杂货店的冰箱黑客攻击升级，暴露联网设备基础安全缺失对关键基础设施的真实风险。

articles.title: Best Wi-Fi Routers (2026): My Honest Picks After Testing 50+
articles.content: Don’t suffer the buffer. These WIRED-tested home routers will deliver reliable internet across your home, whatever your needs or budget.
articles.summary: Wired 实测 50 多款路由器，按需求和预算推荐可覆盖全屋、稳定联网的最佳 Wi-Fi 路由器。

articles.title: Entire's Git Forge Rethinks Git Collaboration for Coding Agents
articles.content: Entire is a Git forge designed specifically for collaboration between human developers and AI coding agents. Its premise is that traditional software development infrastructure, particularly the pull request (PR) model, is not well suited to an environment where AI agents generate, review, and iterate on code at high speed. By Sergio De Simone
articles.summary: Entire 推出面向人类开发者与 AI 编码代理协作的 Git forge，认为传统 PR 模式不适合 AI 生成与评审代码。

articles.title: Google Cloud Adds Self-Managed VMware Cloud Foundation on Bare Metal
articles.content: Google Cloud has made a self-managed VMware solution generally available, running VMware Cloud Foundation 9.x on dedicated Z3 bare metal with root access across ESXi, vCenter and NSX in 22 regions. It sits beside the Google-managed VMware Engine and matches customer-operated offerings from AWS and Oracle, shifting lifecycle, patching and Broadcom licensing back to the customer. By Steef-Jan Wiggers
articles.summary: 谷歌云正式提供自管理 VMware Cloud Foundation 9.x 裸金属方案，覆盖 22 个区域，与 AWS、Oracle 同类服务竞争。

articles.title: Cloudflare Scales D1 Control Plane to Millions of Databases
articles.content: In a recent article, Cloudflare shared the redesign of the control plane of its D1 serverless SQL database to support millions of databases, avoiding centralized bottlenecks, implementing retries and idempotency, and using eventual consistency. By Renato Losio
articles.summary: Cloudflare 重构 D1 无服务器 SQL 数据库控制平面，以支撑数百万数据库，避免集中瓶颈并引入重试与幂等。

articles.title: How Grab Improved Mobile App Stability by Safely Handling Surge in AI-Generated Code Changes
articles.content: The growing adoption of AI coding assistants has accelerated development and increased the volume of code changes per release, bringing more opportunities for defects and crashes, says Grab. To address these challenges, they implemented a layered defense strategy to prevent, detect, and contain crashes throughout the development and release lifecycle. By Sergio De Simone
articles.summary: Grab 针对 AI 编码助手带来的代码变更激增，实施分层防御策略，提升移动应用稳定性、减少崩溃。

articles.title: Open Source pg_vectorsearch Brings More Scalable Vector Search to PostgreSQL
articles.content: Tiger Data has released pg_vectorsearch, an open source PostgreSQL extension for vector similarity search, currently in alpha. Its PRISM index uses data partitioning and compression instead of the graph-based approach used by pgvector’s HNSW index, reducing memory requirements and index build times. By Renato Losio
articles.summary: Tiger Data 发布开源 PostgreSQL 向量搜索扩展 pg_vectorsearch，PRISM 索引以分区压缩降低内存占用和构建时间。

articles.title: Varlock Releases Bumpy: a File-Based Versioning Alternative to Changesets
articles.content: Bumpy is an MIT-licensed, TypeScript tool for version management and changelogs in monorepos. It follows the changesets workflow, using markdown bump files, and adds support for workspace and catalog protocols, custom publish commands, and branch-based prereleases. Changesets v3, released in August 2026, closed many earlier gaps, though differences remain. By Daniel Curtis
articles.summary: Varlock 发布 MIT 许可的 TypeScript 工具 Bumpy，以文件式版本管理替代 Changesets，支持 monorepo 与预发布。

articles.title: Yelp Combines Native and Server-Driven UI for its AI Assistant
articles.content: Yelp combines native mobile controls with server-driven conversation rendering in its AI Assistant using the CHAOS framework. The architecture separates view configuration from conversation data, supports backend-driven chat interactions, and enables faster UI updates without new app releases. Yelp also discusses cross-platform challenges and reuse for its Biz Ask Anything pilot. By Leela Kumili
articles.summary: Yelp 用 CHAOS 框架将原生控件与服务端驱动对话渲染结合，实现 AI 助手 UI 无需发版即可快速更新。

articles.title: GitLab 19.5 Makes Agentic Development a Governed Part of the DevOps Platform
articles.content: GitLab 19.5, released on October 15, puts agentic software development and governance at the centre of the platform, making its GitLab MCP server generally available while expanding how external AI agents can interact with GitLab. By Craig Risi
articles.summary: GitLab 19.5 将代理式开发纳入平台治理，正式开放 MCP 服务器，并扩展外部 AI 代理与 GitLab 的交互方式。

articles.title: TypeScript 7.1 Beta: Restores the Compiler API and Makes Vue and Svelte First-Class
articles.content: TypeScript 7.1 Beta, announced October 20, 2026, restores the compiler API removed in 7.0, now split into separate entry points. It adds content mappers, letting tools like Vue check non-standard files. One Vue project's type checks fell from 14.19 to 3.10 seconds. An editor issue remains open, and teams may need TypeScript 6 alongside 7. By Daniel Curtis
articles.summary: TypeScript 7.1 Beta 恢复 7.0 移除的编译器 API 并拆分入口，新增内容映射器，使 Vue 项目类型检查从 14.19 秒降至 3.10 秒。

articles.title: Presentation: The Socio-Technical Staff+ Engineer: Architecture, Culture and Organisational Change
articles.content: Vanessa Formicola shares how technical leaders can move beyond "wishful architecture" by practicing holistic socio-technical engineering. She discusses why engineering leaders must account for organizational maturity, reward structures, geopolitical climate, and team dynamics, framing the staff-plus role as designing the conditions for technology to thrive rather than just picking tools. By Vanessa Formicola
articles.summary: Vanessa Formicola 分享 Staff+ 工程师如何超越“一厢情愿的架构”，综合组织成熟度、激励结构与团队动态推动变革。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #542: AI week ahead: data center pause backers could win 15 governor races
articles.content: This issue is about the week ahead, and something is scheduled almost every day. On Tuesday, US voters choose 36 governors, and in up to 15 of those races the candidate who backs a pause on new data centers could win. Apple reports earnings today and AMD on Tuesday. On Wednesday, Apple starts testing Apple Intelligence in China with Alibaba's Qwen, and Agility Robotics expects to close its deal to go public. When Congress returns on November 9, OpenAI plans to push for "speed limits" on the most powerful AI. Last week, a fake Claude Code update reached up to 5,000 Cursor users, and in a Cornell and Yale test nine of ten AI models raised their own spending limits. In the middle: insuring Big Tech's debt now costs more than at any time since 2021.
articles.summary: 美国36场州长选举中，最多15场支持暂停新建数据中心的候选人有望胜出，同时苹果、AMD本周发布财报。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #541: Big Tech reports AI spending Wednesday as CoreWeave debt hits distress
articles.content: This issue looks ahead. On Wednesday the Fed announces its rate decision, then Microsoft and Alphabet report after the close. Amazon follows on Thursday. Investors want to know whether AI spending is still paying off, and the credit market is already nervous: insurance against a CoreWeave default now costs more than 10% a year. Anthropic is expected to file its IPO paperwork publicly any day. Moonshot says Kimi K3.1 Pro's open weights arrive November 4. Israel votes on Tuesday after a campaign full of AI deepfakes, and the US midterms are a week from Tuesday. In the middle: so far, AI has paid off for the companies that sell it, not the ones that buy it.
articles.summary: 微软、Alphabet、亚马逊本周发布财报，投资者关注AI支出回报，CoreWeave债务违约保险成本飙升引发信贷市场担忧。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #540: AI is finding software flaws faster than teams can fix them
articles.content: This Applied AI edition looks at what organizations actually did with AI over the past two weeks, drawn from our Use-Case Library and from SEC filings. Three things stand out: AI now finds security flaws at record volume, AI agents do a large share of the work at some companies, and test agents keep doing things nobody asked them to do.
articles.summary: AI发现安全漏洞的速度远超团队修复能力，部分公司AI代理承担大量工作，测试代理持续增多。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #539: AI-made midterm ads top $137 million, and 70% carry no AI label
articles.content: Campaigns and PACs have spent more than $137 million on AI-generated or AI-enhanced midterm ads, and about 70% of them carry no AI label, the New York Times reported. The biggest pro-AI super PAC network paid about $20 million to a Nevada company that exists only as a post office box. A new report found 81 of 134 AI models failed a test built from terrorist-style questions. A video game reverse engineering site is closing because AI made the work too easy. Some companies that rushed into AI are now limiting it, and a JAMA study counted 270 million questions doctors asked one AI tool. In the middle: police in Michigan used an AI-generated photo of a teenager to catch a suspect.
articles.summary: 竞选团队和PAC在AI生成中期选举广告上花费超1.37亿美元，约70%未标注AI，最大亲AI超级PAC向空壳公司支付约2000万美元。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #537: AI models may soon copy themselves onto smart fridges, Anthropic says
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared most since our last issue on October 8, minus the stories we already sent you in the Daily Espresso. The most shared: Anthropic's warning that small AI models may soon be able to copy themselves onto home devices. Also: a large study of what AI coding agents change at real companies, a fight over how to check AI math proofs, creative workers pushing back on AI, and police buying more AI.
articles.summary: Anthropic警告小型AI模型可能很快能自我复制到智能冰箱等家用设备，另有大型研究发布。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #536: Top AI models failed a test of inventing new AI research
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared over the past three days. Most of them look ahead: whether AI can do AI research on its own, who gets a say in governing it, how it is moving into war planning, and how it is moving onto personal computers.
articles.summary: 顶尖AI模型未能通过自主开展新AI研究的测试，同时AI治理话语权和军事规划应用引发关注。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #535: AI got too expensive, so companies are moving to cheaper models
articles.content: This Applied AI edition looks at what organizations actually did with AI over the past three weeks. Three patterns stand out: companies switching models to control cost, large deployments that are now in daily use, and a growing list of places where AI was restricted or removed.
articles.summary: AI成本过高促使企业转向更便宜的模型，大型部署进入日常使用，同时AI受限或被移除的场景增多。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #534: Universities cannot grade their way out of AI
articles.content: This week, campus IT leaders voted AI their top priority for the first time, Cambridge refused Turnitin's new terms over AI training on student work, Dartmouth opened an investigation into its own provost's writing, and Ken Griffin gave Carnegie Mellon $3 billion. Student AI use is no longer a future scenario. The useful question for universities is whether they can teach students to work with AI and still certify what those students can do without it. New evidence from tutoring trials, assessment redesigns, student-support systems and campus data deals points to a practical answer.
articles.summary: 高校IT负责人首次将AI列为首要任务，剑桥拒绝Turnitin新条款，达特茅斯调查教务长写作，AI使用已非未来议题。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #533: Meta tested human callers behind its AI phone agent
articles.content: The AI story of September 22–28 was not simply that agents became more capable. It was that their hidden handoffs became visible: a supposedly automated call could reach a contractor, a supposedly private prompt or image could reach a reviewer, a monitor could detect an agent long before a person stopped it, and a local app flaw could inherit every permission a user had granted. The new AI Weekly Who’s Who census points to one practical question: when an agent crosses a boundary, who knows—and who can still intervene?
articles.summary: Meta的AI电话代理被曝背后有真人接线员，自动化交接、隐私泄露和代理监控问题浮出水面。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #531: AI labs shipped agents before agreeing how to report failures
articles.content: The AI story of September 14–20 was not one spectacular model launch. It was the machinery around agents becoming visible: people reading private chats, models writing instructions into their own memory, plugins updating beneath users, and regulators asking how to stop a system after release. The latest AI Weekly Who’s Who census surfaced 535 expert-shared links. We ranked them by consequence and reader relevance, not by raw share count. Here is what mattered last week—and, more importantly, what could move the story from September 22–28.
articles.summary: AI实验室在未就故障报告达成一致前就发布代理，私人聊天被阅读、模型自写记忆、插件静默更新等问题显现。

articles.title: We now have Kerr’s Law
articles.content: Dave Kerr created hacker laws, and now he finds himself reviewing agent-written code for them. Back on the show after six years, Dave names what he sees limiting teams today: keeping everyone’s mental model in sync with what’s actually been built. Adam declares it Kerr’s Law on the spot. We get into why Dave’s team treats code review as a deliberate slowdown, how Shellwright lets agents bring evidence to a pull request, and what living with bipolar disorder has taught Dave about noticing when the excitement of these tools stops being healthy.
articles.summary: Dave Kerr提出“Kerr定律”，指出团队最大瓶颈是让所有人的心智模型与实际构建保持同步。

articles.title: The future is Postgres
articles.content: Craig Kerstiens returns to talk about the ever-expanding world of Postgres: a deliberately boring core, a thriving extension ecosystem, and pg_lake bringing DuckDB and Iceberg into the mix. We dig into the pain of ETL, what Craig is watching in Postgres 19, the impact of AI on open source maintainers, and why the database still has plenty of room to grow.
articles.summary: Craig Kerstiens谈Postgres扩展生态与pg_lake整合DuckDB和Iceberg，以及AI对开源维护者的影响。

articles.title: Building what's next
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Zeno Rocha, CEO of Resend, about scaling "boring" email to 3 million users, the secret Go rewrite behind it, and building for agents. We cover pricing.md, MCP, spam gangs, and why Resend keeps what's next for email.
articles.summary: Resend CEO Zeno Rocha分享如何用Go重写将“无聊”的邮件服务扩展至300万用户，并为AI代理构建产品。

articles.title: From zero to NanoClaw
articles.content: Gavriel Cohen, creator of NanoClaw and co-founder of NanoCo, joins Adam to explain how a 40-hour weekend project became a viral open source hit and the foundation of an enterprise AI company. Gavriel describes the security concerns that led him to build a small, container-isolated alternative to OpenClaw, why he released it under the MIT license, and why the project's community and credibility are more valuable than keeping its code private. They explore the shift from writing code to architecting the environments in which agents work, NanoClaw's "skills over features" approach, the approval and governance layers required inside large companies, and a future where every worker manages agents without surrendering human judgment. They close with the technical simplicity behind NanoClaw, containers, TypeScript, SQLite, and a two-database design, and Adam's case for durable Agent Flow artifacts that keep organizational context from disappearing into chat.
articles.summary: Gavriel Cohen的40小时周末项目NanoClaw成为病毒式开源爆款，并发展为容器隔离的企业AI公司。

On Thursday, September 17th, Changelog is taking over PlanetScale’s HQ in San Francisco for an evening of short talks and conversations about AI, developer tools and what people are building. articles.title: Forking Cal.com to closed source
articles.content: This week I'm joined by Peer Richelsen, co-founder of Cal.com. What if the majority of open source repositories are already compromised and we just don't know it yet? That's the theory Peer brings to the table this week. We dig into how AI has flattened the knowledge graph to the point that a 16-year-old can vibe hack a power station just as easily as their mom can vibe code an iOS app, why the reporting culture that has kept open source safe all these years is collapsing under AI generated noise, Cal.com's move to fork its own codebase and take the sensitive parts private, and the eye opening reality that shipping "$1 of AI tokens for pennies on the dollar" is now a common startup business model.
articles.summary: Cal.com联合创始人Peer Richelsen提出多数开源仓库可能已被攻陷，并讨论AI如何压平知识图谱。

articles.title: Postgres at PlanetScale
articles.content: Sam Lambert is back after 4 years and he does not hold back! We cover $5 PlanetScale Postgres, the Neki "do-over" of Vitess, agents shipping schema changes through deploy requests, rolling back a 500TB table in seconds, and the very real question of whether to open source any of it. Plus: why he thinks the sleeping, lazy giants should be broken up.
articles.summary: PlanetScale CEO Sam Lambert谈5美元Postgres、Vitess重写、代理通过部署请求提交模式变更及500TB表秒级回滚。

articles.title: Canary tokens and digital tripwires
articles.content: Haroon Meer is back! Haroon is the Founder of Thinkst, the ~50-person bootstrapped company behind Canary and Canarytokens — honeypots and tripwires you sprinkle inside your network and forget about until an attacker touches one. We talk about the AWS API key token attackers just can't resist trying, the real credit card token backed by an actual bank partnership, Breadcrumbs (their brand-new feature that leads intruders straight to your canaries), a live demo where a hardware Canary becomes a Synology NAS in one click, and how a company with zero outbound sales and no price increase in ten years quietly passed $22.5 million in ARR.
articles.summary: Thinkst创始人Haroon Meer介绍Canary蜜罐和数字绊线，以及攻击者难以抗拒尝试的AWS API密钥令牌。

articles.title: From open source hits to OpenAI
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Max Stoiber, currently working on ChatGPT's plugin directory and app platform at OpenAI. We discuss the hundreds of open source projects nobody remembers alongside the big ones like react-boilerplate and styled-components, how Spectrum became part of GitHub and eventually helped shape GitHub Discussions, the founder growth that came from building Stellate, the GraphQL cache that turned into a dual acquisition by Shopify and The Guild, and why ChatGPT apps feel like a new surface for software.
articles.summary: Max Stoiber回顾react-boilerplate等开源项目历程，现于OpenAI负责ChatGPT插件目录和应用平台。

articles.title: MCP on Code Mode
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Matt Carey about Code Mode and how most of us have been thinking about MCP all wrong. Matt works on the Agents SDK and MCP at Cloudflare — we discuss how server-side Code Mode lets one MCP server expose all ~2,500 Cloudflare API endpoints in about 1,000 tokens of context, the dynamic Worker loader that runs model-written code safely in a V8 isolate, Matt's own workflow with Claude, where memory fits into the future of agents, and his Zaggy git wrapper that keeps agents from force-pushing his repos.
articles.summary: Cloudflare的Matt Carey讲解服务端Code Mode如何用约1000个token暴露全部约2500个API端点。

articles.title: Can CrowdStrike's New 'AI Kill Switch' Shut Down Rogue AI Agents?
articles.content: CrowdStrike's "Falcon Guardian" protects Windows systems by enforcing policy, restricting unauthorized applications and blocking USB devices, notes Gartner. And now CrowdStrike says they're giving security teams "the ultimate human control over AI agents" with — an "AI Kill Switch... a defender can terminate it where it runs, block it from launching again, and cut off its enterprise network access." "When you deploy agents with a kill switch, you stay in control," said George Kurtz, CEO and founder of CrowdStrike... "The AI Kill Switch puts power in the hands of the people to realize AI safety...." In the case of a rogue agent, the AI Kill Switch will give the security decision-maker the final control: terminate the agent at its root, where it runs. It starts on the endpoint, where the Falcon sensor already operates, and builds on what Falcon Guardian already sees: what an agent is told to do, what it communicates, and what it executes... An authorized administrator triggers the action, and every action is recorded in the audit trail. CrowdStrike also announced it's acquiring Fiddler AI, a company it describes as "a leader in AI agent observability and explainability" that will give their Falcon platform "pre-deployment evaluation, continuous behavioral accountability, and agent explainability." Together with the Falcon Guardian innovations announced today, CrowdStrike will deliver comprehensive AI security and AI safety: Guardian secures agents from attack and misuse; Fiddler validates they behaved as intended. "Every company is deploying agents and asking the same thing: what are agents actually doing?" said George Kurtz, CEO and founder of CrowdStrike. "When a regulator or your board asks what an agent did, saying 'the model did it' is not an answer. Fiddler is the flight recorder for every agent: the observability to explain exactly what an agent did and why. This level of agent visibility and control enables AI safety." AI agents are goal-seeking. They hit an o
articles.summary: CrowdStrike推出Falcon Guardian的“AI终止开关”，让安全团队可强制关闭失控AI代理，强化Windows系统策略管控。

articles.title: Nvidia CEO Admits Affair With Alleged Chinese Spy. Investigation Opened
articles.content: CNBC reports new details about the relationship of alleged Chinese spy with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang: Huang told Nvidia staff in a email on Sunday that he had an affair with the woman and that Nvidia's board of directors had opened an independent investigation into the spying allegations. "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did," Huang wrote in the message. "I am deeply sorry." Nvidia's board "said an independent committee, assisted by outside counsel, will investigate the matter," reports Axios: The board said it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised and expressed confidence in Huang's leadership... Huang has been a key voice in Washington pushing to loosen restrictions on AI chip sales to China. He argued that keeping American technology in the Chinese market strengthens U.S. competitiveness and prevented China from developing their own potentially more advanced chips. The board's statement added that their inquiry "will examine all available information," CNBC reports. But "An Nvidia spokesperson said that Huang was committed to continuing as CEO of Nvidia without interruption." "I love our country and our company," Jensen Huang wrote in his letter to Nvidia's staff (as reported by CNBC), "and I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American." But while U.S. lawmakers have requested Huang appear for closed-door committee briefing, Jensen has not confirmed he'll appear, notes CNBC: When asked by the New York Times whether Huang would appear before lawmakers to discuss the matter, Nvidia spokesman John Rizzo declined to comment. "Our chief executive has an outstanding security team that accompanies him where needed," Mr. Rizzo said in a statement to the Times... Rizzo said [Thursday] the Nvidia CEO's interactions with [alleged Chinese spy Alice] Huang were consistent with meetings he has had w
articles.summary: 英伟达CEO黄仁勋承认与一名被指中国间谍的女子有婚外情，董事会已就间谍指控启动独立调查。

articles.title: Parents Sue Google Over AI Safety Risks On School Chromebooks
articles.content: The New York Times reports: After chatting for months with Google's artificial intelligence on a school-issued Chromebook laptop, a 13-year-old student made plans to end her life, according to a lawsuit filed in California Superior Court on Monday, the latest in a wave of litigation over Big Tech's effects on young people. The lawsuit, which refers to the girl as Emma, said that her parents first learned she had access to Google's AI in mid-March after their daughter's school sent a message warning them that she was in "imminent danger" of self-harm. Emma's mother logged into the teen's school Google account and found her daughter composing a suicide note on Google Docs, the complaint said. Her parents, named as John and Jane Doe in the lawsuit, immediately took Emma for an emergency psychiatric evaluation, and she now goes to therapy every week. Emma, a seventh grader in Charlotte, North Carolina, had grown convinced that she had multiple mental health disorders following interactions with AI Mode, a chatbotlike feature on Google Search, the complaint said. She also searched for "what is a suicide note" and made comments like "I am planning my own funeral" to the AI, the complaint said. The lawsuit is likely the first to claim that Google "hastily integrated" AI features into company apps used on K-12 Chromebooks, Google-powered laptops provided to millions of children by U.S. school districts, while failing to notify their parents of the potential risks... The case underscores how public school districts have come to depend on classroom laptops, tablets and apps from companies like Google and Microsoft for teaching and learning. In recent years, some Big Tech companies have used their own infrastructure in schools to promote their AI chatbots for teachers and students. The new lawsuit argues that Google's "sprawling digital ecosystem" of laptops and apps has enabled the tech giant to spread its Gemini AI chatbot across public schools — as well as turn on some stud
articles.summary: 一名13岁学生与谷歌AI长时间对话后计划自杀，家长在加州起诉谷歌，指其校园Chromebook上的AI存在安全风险。

articles.title: Salon, One of the Web's Pioneering News Outlets, Shuts Down After 31 Years
articles.content: "It has been an extraordinary privilege," says the subheading on Thursday's announcement. After 31 years Salon.com will stop publishing, according to an announcement which appeared on the site under the byline "Salon". articles.title: Do Data Centers Have a Smaller Effect on Electricity Prices Than We Think?
articles.content: "According to a new study by researchers at Harvard University and the University of Pennsylvania, data centers are probably having only a small effect on residential electricity prices," reports the Washington Post. "The researchers calculated that these operations were responsible for just 4% of the utility rate increases over the last five years..." There are certainly some areas — like in Pennsylvania, Virginia, Ohio and other states covered by grid operator PJM — where data centers have skyrocketed demand, pushing some costs onto residential customers. But multiple studies by different researchers and organizations have failed to find a strong connection between data centers and the overall trajectory of U.S. electricity prices in recent years. Another analysis earlier this year by researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology found that, between 2010 and 2024, data centers increased average electricity prices for residential customers by just 2.1%. Last year, research from the Brattle Group and Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory found that data centers were actually decreasing costs in certain regions. And another study by the Electric Power Research Institute found that a doubling of data center capacity between 2019 and 2024 resulted in a 4 percent drop in home electricity prices... The new Harvard and Penn study found a slightly higher impact on industrial electricity prices — the price paid by manufacturers and large facilities. For those customers, data centers were responsible for 15% of the price increase between 2020 and 2025. But for ordinary Americans... the changes simply were not substantial [according to Wharton School professor Serguei Netessine, one of the study's authors]. "So far we have no evidence that data centers increase prices all that much," Netessine said. articles.title: Dual JWT Authentication: Security, Redis, and Trade-Offs
articles.content: Authentication is one of those backend features that looks simple until you need to make it secure, scalable, and inexpensive. A user logs in, receives a token, and includes it in subsequent requests. The server verifies the token and allows access. Easy enough. But real applications need more than that. Users expect to stay signed in for weeks, log out from multiple devices, recover from interrupted connections, and have their sessions terminated when credentials are compromised. Meanwhile, backend teams want to avoid unnecessary database queries on every authenticated request. These requirements pull authentication architecture in different directions. One possible compromise is a Dual JWT architecture : short-lived access tokens sent through the Authorization header, longer-lived refresh tokens stored in secure cookies, and a small Redis-backed mechanism for revoking sessions. The approach can reduce database traffic significantly. But its security properties depend on how refresh tokens are managed, how revocation works, and which attacks the application needs to defend against. Let’s examine the architecture, its implementation in Node.js, and the trade-offs that are easy to overlook. 1. Why a Single Token Is Often Not Enough Consider an application that uses one JWT for authentication. After login, the server issues a token: Authorization : Bearer eyJhbGciOi... Every protected API request includes that token. The server verifies its signature and expiration time without querying a session database. This is convenient, but the token’s lifetime creates a problem. If it expires after 15 minutes, users need a way to obtain another token without repeatedly entering their credentials. If it remains valid for 30 days, stealing it may give an attacker access for a long time. Neither option is particularly attractive. What About Cookie-Based Sessions? Traditional session authentication usually stores an opaque session identifier in an HttpOnly cookie. The browser sends that cookie automatically, and the server looks up the associated session. This approach has important advantages. Tokens aren’t exposed to ordinary JavaScript through document.cookie , and individual sessions can be invalidated centrally. However, cookie-based authentication also requires appropriate CSRF defenses because browsers attach eligible cookies automatically. That doesn’t make cookie sessions inherently insecure. Properly implemented server-side sessions remain an excellent choice for many web applications. The question is whether the application needs the additional flexibility of separate access and refresh credentials. 2. Two Tokens, Two Responsibilities The Dual JWT approach separates API access from session renewal. articles.title: pathmask matches relative paths against patterns in the syntax of .gitignore
articles.content: Match relative paths against patterns in the syntax of .gitignore . pathmask checks paths as text and never reads the file system. Use it to filter a list of files the way git does. Required Node.js 22 or newer. The mask matches logs except keep.log , and the folder tmp with all its content: import { PathMask } from 'pathmask' ; const mask = new PathMask ( [ '*.log' , '!keep.log' , 'tmp/' ] ) ; mask . matches ( 'error.log' ) ; // true mask . matches ( 'keep.log' ) ; // false mask . matches ( 'tmp/' ) ; // true mask . matches ( 'tmp/cache/a.json' ) ; // true mask . matches ( 'src/index.js' ) ; // false Creates a mask from the lines of a .gitignore file. Parameter Type Description patterns string[] The lines of the mask, see Patterns and Lines . Throws a TypeError when patterns is not an array of strings. Checks one path. Parameter Type Description path string A path relative to the root of the mask, see Paths . Returns true when the mask matches the path or a folder that contains it. Throws a TypeError when the path is empty, starts with / , or has an empty part, . or .. . The constructor reads the patterns, matches() only checks the path. Create one mask and use it for all paths: const ignored = new PathMask ( [ 'node_modules/' , '*.log' , '.*' ] ) ; const paths = [ 'README.md' , 'debug.log' , '.env' , 'src/index.js' , 'node_modules/ansis/index.js' ] ; const files = paths . filter ( ( file ) => ! ignored . matches ( file ) ) ; // ['README.md', 'src/index.js'] Filter the files of a folder This example reads all files of the folder my-project and its subfolders, then keeps the files that the mask does not match. The folder has the same files as the list above. import { readdir } from 'node:fs/promises' ; import path from 'node:path' ; import { PathMask } from 'pathmask' ; const rootPath = './my-project' ; const ignored = new PathMask ( [ 'node_modules/' , '*.log' , '.*' ] ) ; const entries = await readdir ( rootPath , { recursive : true , withFileTypes : true } ) ; const files = [ ] ; for ( const entry of entries ) { if ( ! entry . isFile ( ) ) continue ; // PathMask needs a path relative to the root. const file = path . relative ( rootPath , path . join ( entry . parentPath , entry . name ) ) ; if ( ! ignored . matches ( file ) ) { files . push ( file ) ; } } // ['README.md', 'src/index.js'] A mask can also pick the files to keep. Here the mask matches the JavaScript files of src and all Markdown files: const selected = new PathMask ( [ 'src/**/*.js' , '*.md' ] ) ; const paths = [ 'README.md' , 'docs/guide.md' , 'package.json' , 'src/index.js' , 'src/cli/run.js' , 'test/run.test.js' ] ; const files = paths . filter ( ( file ) => selected . matches ( file ) ) ; // ['README.md', 'docs/guide.md', 'src/index.js', 'src/cli/run.js'] With /*.md only the Markdown files of the root are matched: README.md , without docs/guide.md . articles.title: Announcing Parcel 3 Alpha
articles.content: Announcing Parcel 3 alpha 2026-11-04 Today we're releasing the first alpha of Parcel 3, a ground up rewrite of Parcel in Rust. It is up to 100x faster than v2, and supports native plugins written in Rust, Go, Swift, or C, as well as a custom runtime for JavaScript and TypeScript plugins. It also includes improved automatic code splitting, library mode, tree shaking, centralized configuration, and much more. Why a rewrite? In Parcel v2, we rewrote several individual pieces of Parcel in Rust. First was our JavaScript compiler , built on top of SWC. Then, we built Lightning CSS . Later, we rebuilt our HTML and SVG transformer and optimizers. However, Parcel's core was still written in JavaScript. This limited our maximum possible performance due to lack of shared memory between threads, high memory usage, garbage collection, and the cost of serializing values between workers and languages. Parcel v3 is an entirely self-contained Rust binary, with no dependency on Node at all. Everything from the CLI and dev server, to the transformers, bundler, optimizers, and everything in between is now fully native. This enables us to efficiently take full advantage of modern multi-core hardware. The results speak for themselves: up to 100x faster builds using the same underlying compilers as v2, only changing the core. Performance Let's cut to the benchmarks. Here's a comparison of cold development builds between v2 and v3 for React Spectrum , a large TypeScript monorepo. articles.title: We Migrated 10,144 Tests from Jest to Vitest in 3 Weeks: The Honest, AI-Assisted Truth
articles.content: A note on the Vitest version: This migration was carried out in August 2026, using Vitest 4 . All the figures, benchmarks, configuration details, and lessons described in this article refer to Vitest 4, not Vitest 5. Migrating a test runner is rarely a magic "swap and go" operation. Our experience moving our entire frontend test suite from Jest to Vitest was a real engineering undertaking, filled with bottlenecks, meticulous pool tuning, unmasked bugs, one rollback, and one optimization we shipped and then had to take back. Over the course of about three weeks, our frontend team migrated eight repositories. We didn't settle for file counts; we ran every suite end-to-end to get the real numbers. Here is the exact scale of what we achieved: 10,144 executed unit tests, real numbers from actually running the suites, not file counts. 1,799 test files across 8 repositories. 0 repos left in a half-migrated state. ~3 weeks to complete the entire effort, migrations plus the tuning that followed. ~$751 estimated AI token cost for the Claude Code sessions we could trace to this work. See the caveats on that number below: it's a rough upper bound, not a bill. This is the story of what actually happened, drawn directly from our git history, PR bodies, and session logs, to help you navigate your own migration. To save you some of the pain we went through, we also published a generalized version of the AI automation skill we ended up wishing we'd had from day one: github.com/Subito-it/articles-code/tree/main/jest-to-vitest-migration . Why Jest started hurting We didn't decide to migrate just because "Jest is slow" in the abstract. We migrated because maintaining it had become an active, recurring tax on our engineering time. We also wanted to be on the side of where the ecosystem was heading, since Vitest was fast becoming the default choice for new Vite/Next.js projects. 1. The CommonJS vs. ESM nightmare By default, next/jest skips transforming anything inside node_modules , so when a dependency ships an ESM-only update, Jest's CommonJS require() fails. We found ourselves hand-patching transformIgnorePatterns regexes to allow-list specific packages. Here's the exact code comment from our config, verbatim: // ESM-only node_modules that Jest must transform. next/jest overwrites any // user-supplied transformIgnorePatterns to skip all of node_modules, so we // allow-list these on the resolved config instead. const esmPackagesToTransform = [ ' cookie ' ]; Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Separately, and about six weeks before we'd even decided to migrate: a major version bump of uuid shipped as pure ESM and broke Jest outright. The real commit message: "uuid v14 ships as pure ESM which breaks Jest (CommonJS). Replace the single usage of uuid() ... with the native crypto.randomUUID() ... removing the dependency entirely." Rather than fight the transform config again, the team just deleted the dependency. When your test runner is dictating your dependency
